metadata.name: dirname
metadata.displayName: dirname - Strip last component from file name
metadata.description: Strip last component from file name (get directory path)

installation.note: dirname is a built-in command available on all Linux systems by default

overview.summary: The dirname command removes the last component from a file path, returning the directory portion. It's the complement to basename - while basename gets the filename, dirname gets the directory path. Commonly used in scripts to determine where a file is located.
when_to_use: Extract directory path from a full file path
Get the parent directory of a file
Determine where a script or file is located

syntax.description: Remove the last component from NAME (the filename), returning the directory path. If NAME contains no slashes, output '.' (current directory).

options.description: End each output line with NUL, not newline
options.use_case: Use with xargs -0 for handling paths with spaces

examples.description: Get the directory path without the filename

output_explanation.notes: dirname removes the last component (the filename), leaving the directory path.

misconceptions.title: dirname only works on files
misconceptions.misconception: dirname only works on file paths, not directory paths
misconceptions.reality: dirname works on any path string - it just removes the last component. For '/path/to/dir/', it returns '/path/to'.
misconceptions.tip: dirname processes any path string, whether it points to a file or directory

misconceptions.title: dirname changes directories
misconceptions.misconception: dirname changes the current working directory
misconceptions.reality: dirname only outputs a string - it doesn't change directories. Use cd with dirname's output to actually change directories.
misconceptions.tip: dirname is for string manipulation. Use 'cd $(dirname path)' to actually change directories.

common_pitfalls.description: Paths with spaces will be split by the shell
dirname /path/dir returns /path, but /path/dir/ also returns /path (trailing slash is part of last component)
common_pitfalls.solution: Be aware that trailing slashes are treated as part of the last component

related_commands.relationship: Complementary; basename gets filename, dirname gets directory
related_commands.description: Strip directory and suffix from filenames

related_commands.relationship: Navigation; often used with dirname to change to a file's directory
Path information; pwd shows current directory, dirname extracts from paths

best_practices: Always quote paths in scripts: dirname "$filepath"
Use with basename to split paths into components
Common pattern: SCRIPT_DIR=$(dirname "$0") to get script's directory
Combine with cd to navigate to a file's directory: cd $(dirname file)
Remember dirname doesn't change directories - it only outputs strings
performance_tips: dirname is very fast - negligible performance impact
For multiple paths, process in a loop rather than calling dirname multiple times separately
Use in scripts for path manipulation without external dependencies

additional_notes.path_manipulation: dirname is part of path manipulation tools including basename and realpath
additional_notes.scripting: Extremely common in shell scripts, especially for getting script locations
additional_notes.complement: Always used together with basename - one gets directory, other gets filename
additional_notes.trailing_slashes: Trailing slashes are treated as part of the last component
